<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }

    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">cua-speedrun</span>: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Pranjal Aggarwal

          <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>

</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Computer use agents (CUAs), which use graphical user interfaces (GUIs) to complete tasks on a computer, have recently surpassed human performance on many standard benchmarks, including difficult long-horizon tasks. Their capabilities are undoubtedly impressive,
however, a key barrier to the widespread adoption and deployment of CUAs remains their speed and cost.
Progress towards faster yet capable CUAs requires reliable evaluation of their speed, but many CUA benchmarks currently face a reproducibility crisis.
Benchmarks are based on complex infrastructure with varying machine and container configurations that confound the evaluation of the execution speed of CUAs. Towards addressing this gap, we propose <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">cua-speedrun</span>, which introduces standardized infrastructure and task sets, with a focus on evaluating the speed and efficiency of CUAs.
<span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">cua-speedrun</span> uses a uniform virtual machine setup and execution pipeline, along with a common agent interface that enables single-agent implementations to operate seamlessly across different benchmarks.
Across four different CUA benchmarks, we evaluate how reasoning effort, agent harnesses, and environment latency affect performance, speed, and cost. We find no single model family is optimal for all three; none of the open-weight models are on the frontier, and also, unintuitively, for some models increasing the reasoning effort can speed up task completion, while faster environment input-output can slow down overall task completion time. We also demonstrate that we can effectively reduce the evaluation task set of most CUA benchmarks without degrading overall statistical power, allowing for more efficient benchmarking and comparison.
We believe <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">cua-speedrun</span> will enable structured progress towards fast, efficient CUAs, unlocking new real-world use cases and applications.
All code, infrastructure, and analysis are available at <a href="https://cuaspeedrun.com" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href"><span class="ltx_ref ltx_nolink">cuaspeedrun.com</span></a>.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_top">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:0.0pt;height:24.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"></span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Computer use agents (CUAs) are language model agents that interact with graphical user interfaces (GUIs) to achieve a user-specified goal. CUAs operate over the same user interface as human users, enabling them to potentially automate a much wider variety of tasks without software-specific APIs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">When measured in terms of success alone, recent model releases have pushed the capabilities of CUAs past human baselines.
The best frontier models today achieve success metrics above human performance on popular CUA benchmarks: Qwen3.8-Max, Claude Mythos 5, GPT-5.5, and Gemini 3.6 Flash report successes ranging from 78.7% to 86.1% on OSWorld-Verified, far above the 72.4% human reference score <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Across long-horizon benchmarks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Aggarwal et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2026b</a>)</cite>, frontier models have also demonstrated the ability to achieve strong performance on complex, long-horizon tasks.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.40284v1/cua-speedrun-scene.svg" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/272;" width="548" height="272"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">cua-speedrun<span id="S1.F1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif"> overview.</span></span>
<span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">cua-speedrun</span> is a standardized platform for benchmarking the performance, speed, and cost of computer-use agents.
It combines representative task selection with standardized infrastructure on Modal, enabling consistent comparisons across models, agent harnesses, and reasoning settings. Our findings reveal that more reasoning can reduce both task time and model cost for CUAs, while faster environment I/O can make agents slower.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Despite their strong performance, a major bottleneck for widespread adoption of current CUAs in practical settings is their speed and cost of deployment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abhyankar et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
In particular, we believe that research on the speed and cost efficiency of CUAs has trailed capabilities research, in part due to the difficulty of fairly benchmarking speed and cost of different models in a consistent manner.
Specifically, CUAs require complex infrastructure to run and evaluate.
Different benchmarks use varying execution environments, ranging from local virtual machines to cloud-parallelized desktops <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bonatti et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
There are drastic differences in deployment setup, API interfaces, hyperparameter settings, agent harnesses, and even benchmark implementations across the community.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Towards addressing the problem of consistent benchmarking of CUA wall-time, and igniting research on improving the speed and deployment practicality of CUAs, we propose <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">cua-speedrun</span>: a standardized platform that can use existing benchmarks to measure the speed and cost efficiency of CUAs (Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).
There are several challenges that <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">cua-speedrun</span> addresses, towards standardizing the evaluation of CUAs across different model families (in particular on wall-time metrics):</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Uniform CUA evaluation infrastructure.</span> We standardize evaluations through a serverless cloud-based provider<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
                  <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
                  
                  
                  
                <a href="https://modal.com/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://modal.com/</a></span></span></span>, where all evaluations run on the exact same execution pipeline and the same virtual machine setup.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Common agent interfaces.</span> Existing CUA implementations are varied and do not always follow the optimal scaffolds. We implement a common agent interface for executing actions and interacting with the environment while allowing for portable agent harnesses and implementations. This allows a single agent implementation to work across different benchmarks. Our analysis also measures time differences due to factors such as the latency of closed-source models, which can vary by provider.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A maximally representative subset for fast and comparable evaluations.</span> CUA benchmarks take a long time to run. We propose an energy minimization framework that selects a minimal representative subset of tasks within existing CUA benchmarks. This allows us to minimize end-to-end evaluation time while preserving the signal of the results, and maintain the relative ordering of agent performance. Our approach reduces evaluation time on OSWorld by 84.9% while maintaining high correlation with evals run on the full set.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We implement these features on <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">cua-speedrun</span>, and benchmark current frontier CUA models on several widely adopted CUA benchmarks, such as OSWorld-Verified <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and OSWorld 2.0 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
In addition, we also perform evaluations and analysis on CUA-World <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Aggarwal et al., 2026</a>)</cite> and MyPCBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2026a</a>)</cite>, which test for long-horizon and personalized computer use, respectively.
<span id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">cua-speedrun</span> allows us to maintain a live Pareto ranking of the most cost-effective, fastest, and most capable models.
Through an extensive analysis of multiple <span id="S1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">cua-speedrun</span> runs, we identify several interesting and applicable insights. Success alone hides large differences in speed: on OSWorld, the open-weight Kimi K3 (max reasoning) matches GPT-6 Astra (high), but takes <math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="4.4\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4.4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.4\times</annotation></semantics></math> longer per task, and none of the open-weight models we evaluate (Kimi K3, MiniMax M3, GLM-5V Turbo) lie on the performance–time or performance–cost Pareto frontier of any benchmarks.
Speed also interacts with reasoning in unintuitive ways: raising reasoning effort can improve benchmark scores while <em id="S1.p5.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">reducing</em> task completion time, since the added reasoning avoids repeated unsuccessful actions. Using a fast I/O system can also slow agents, as the models have not been trained to interact with desktops in different I/O speed configurations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Our findings highlight the importance of turning our attention beyond performance and success rates. <span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">cua-speedrun</span> maintains a standardized evaluation of the performance and efficiency of CUAs, two dimensions that we believe are essential future research directions. We hope that the public release of <span id="S1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">cua-speedrun</span> encourages the research community to work on making CUAs faster, cheaper, and more efficient, paving the way towards more widespread real-world adoption.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Method</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we describe our approach to address the aforementioned challenges with benchmarking CUAs. We base our techniques to improve CUA benchmarking on standardizing measurements and infrastructure (Sec. <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 Standardized Computer-Use Evaluation ‣ 2 Method ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>), selecting representative tasks instead of running entire benchmarks (Sec. <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Selecting a Representative Set ‣ 2 Method ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>), and building infrastructure that executes and times every agent consistently (Sec. <a href="#S2.SS3" title="2.3 Infrastructure ‣ 2 Method ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Standardized Computer-Use Evaluation</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Standardizing computer-use evaluations requires invariance across four different dimensions: (1) the agent, driven by a large-language-model; (2) the benchmark,
which determines what an agent must accomplish; (3) the environment infrastructure, which is responsible for managing VMs, the environment lifecycle, and action/observation contracts; and (4) the agent loop, which determines
how the model interacts with the infrastructure. Many computer-use evaluations often make different choices for these four components, making it difficult to study them independently. For example, adopting a new model may introduce a benchmark-specific
action loop, or adopting a new benchmark requires changes to the agent or infrastructure.
The goal of our setup is to ensure the decoupling of benchmarks from infrastructure from agent design, in order to ensure fair and independent evaluation across these four dimensions.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Problem setup.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following prior computer-use benchmarks, each task specifies an initial desktop state, a natural-language instruction, and a verifier, either a programmatic check or an LLM judge, that scores the agent’s trajectory and final state. Agents observe screenshots of the desktop and act through keyboard and mouse actions; Appendix <a href="#A10.SS1" title="J.1 Task Definition ‣ Appendix J Experimental Details ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">J.1</span></a> gives the formal definition. Comparisons between agents hold the benchmark and infrastructure fixed, and similarly comparisons across benchmarks fix agent and infrastructure, so each change behaves as a clean ablation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Measuring speed.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each task, our infrastructure starts measuring time when the instruction is given to the agent and
stops when the agent terminates or reaches the task limit (steps taken, wall-time, or both). Environment
provisioning, task setup, agent initialization, and verification occur outside
of this interval. The infrastructure records the total task time and additionally separates it into the time spent executing environment operations and the time spent executing agent operations. Thus, the agent time can be fully attributed to the “speed” of the agent, regardless of any time needed to set up CUA evaluations. Additionally,
we also log the total cost of model calls. In addition, infra failures are retried,
while agent failures end the trajectory, which is then scored.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Selecting a Representative Set</h3>

<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Choosing a representative evaluation set.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A full computer-use evaluation is often expensive because of long trajectories adding to API/GPU cost, and often requires overhead for managing virtual machines (VMs), adding substantial evaluation cost. For example, GPT-5.4 costs approximately
$4000 on the CUA-World-Long benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Aggarwal et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. We therefore ask the question: can we reduce the size of the
benchmark needed for eval, while still capturing the success rate of the agents we evaluate on the full set?
We want to choose a subset that keeps the individual agents’ scores similar to their full benchmark scores and
preserves the ordering of agents’ performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Selection criteria based on success.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our goal is to automatically select a subset <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> of the benchmark that is representative of the full benchmark. To ensure that the selected subset generalizes beyond the agents used to construct it, we evaluate the selection procedure using leave-one-agent-out validation. For each agent <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math>, we construct a subset using the results of only the other agents (M-1) and then compare the held-out agent’s score on the selected subset with its score on the full benchmark.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We found through multiple iterations of leave-one-model-out evaluation that the best method to select tasks was to minimize the energy distance between the distributions of agent
scores on the full benchmark and subset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Székely and Rizzo, 2013</a>)</cite>. Specifically, let <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{mi}\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{mi}\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> be the partial score of agent <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> on task <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, and let
<math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="B_{mi}=\mathbf{1}[C_{mi}=1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟏</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{mi}=\mathbf{1}[C_{mi}=1]</annotation></semantics></math> denote exact completion. We represent task <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>
by</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{i}=(C_{1i},\ldots,C_{Mi},B_{1i},\ldots,B_{Mi})\in\mathbb{R}^{2M}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{i}=(C_{1i},\ldots,C_{Mi},B_{1i},\ldots,B_{Mi})\in\mathbb{R}^{2M}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Thus, two tasks are considered similar when agents exhibit similar patterns of partial and exact completion on them. Let <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{ij}=\lVert z_{i}-z_{j}\rVert_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><msub><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{ij}=\lVert z_{i}-z_{j}\rVert_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> and let
<math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\overline{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\overline{D}</annotation></semantics></math> be the mean distance between distinct tasks. For a subset
<math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{K}</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> tasks, we minimize</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></munder><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>N</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><msup><mi>j</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>j</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="2.100em" minsize="2.100em">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{split}\mathcal{E}(S_{K})=\frac{1}{\overline{D}}\bigg(&amp;\frac{2}{KN}\sum_{i\in S_{K}}\sum_{j=1}^{N}D_{ij}-\frac{1}{K^{2}}\sum_{i,i^{\prime}\in S_{K}}D_{ii^{\prime}}-\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\sum_{j^{\prime}=1}^{N}D_{jj^{\prime}}\bigg).\end{split}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">This objective favors subsets whose tasks represent the performance patterns present in the full benchmark while avoiding redundant tasks with nearly identical patterns. The final term depends only on the full benchmark and is therefore constant during subset selection. We approximately
minimize this objective by starting with 100 task subsets and replacing one
selected task with an unselected task whenever this reduces the objective.
Thus, we retain the subset with the lowest objective value across the 100 runs. During leave-one-agent-out evaluation, this procedure is repeated after removing the held-out agent’s results. After determining the desired subset size, we construct the final deployed subset once using all available agents.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">What subset is sufficient to preserve model rankings?</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The previous selection criteria can find the representative set for a given value of <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>. Next, we ask for the smallest subset of <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> tasks that consistently preserves
the ranking of agents by performance. Let <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{q}(K)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{q}(K)</annotation></semantics></math>
be the Spearman correlation between leave-one-agent-out estimates and full benchmark
results for evaluation quantity <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math>. We choose</p>
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K^{*}=\min\left\{K:\min_{q}\min_{k\in\{K-1,K,K+1\}}\rho_{q}(k)\geq 0.95\right\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><mi>q</mi></munder><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><munder><mi>min</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></munder></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mn>0.95</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K^{*}=\min\left\{K:\min_{q}\min_{k\in\{K-1,K,K+1\}}\rho_{q}(k)\geq 0.95\right\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">We require the correlation threshold to hold for (K-1), (K), and (K+1) to prevent us from selecting a value of (K) that performs well only by chance.
This criterion selects 50 of 295 OSWorld tasks, 52 of 63 OSWorld2 tasks,
26 of 143 CUA-World tasks, and 38 of 184 MyPCBench tasks
(Table <a href="#A7.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ Appendix G Representative Task Selection ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>), which form the
<span id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">cua-speedrun</span> evaluation sets. We also evaluate how well the subsets preserve full-benchmark performance and model comparisons in our experiments (Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Representative Task Selection ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Infrastructure</h3>

<section id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">How do we host our infrastructure?</h5>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We adapt the virtual machine runtime from
Gym-Anything <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Aggarwal et al., 2026</a>)</cite> to run task environments natively
in Modal sandboxes. Our infrastructure manages separate sandboxes for agents
and environments, ensuring isolation, while Modal sandboxes provide a
standardized hosted runtime so that differences in users’ infrastructure do
not affect evaluation results. For self-hosted open-weight models, we use vLLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwon et al., 2023</a>)</cite> inference
servers on fixed L40S GPUs. Keeping the inference servers and GPUs fixed allows consistency in evaluation. We develop a Python library to handle GPU scheduling,
environment allocation, and parallelization, with further details in
Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Infrastructure: Technical Details ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Action and observation modalities.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following standard practice in computer-use agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, the action space consists of keyboard actions (e.g., typing text or pressing
<span id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Ctrl+C</span>) and mouse actions (e.g., clicking at coordinates <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,y)</annotation></semantics></math> or
double-clicking). Agent observations are RGB screenshots of the desktop at a
resolution of <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1920\times 1080" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1920</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>1080</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1920\times 1080</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To ensure that these interfaces behave consistently across VM runtimes, we
developed <span id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">CUA-AutoDebug</span>, an end-to-end test suite in which a
controlled application records the keyboard and mouse inputs it receives,
compares them with the intended inputs for a large catalog of actions, and
checks that screenshots match the application state. These tests uncovered
several input errors in widely used CUA tools, which we correct in our
infrastructure (Appendix <a href="#A9" title="Appendix I Validating Actions with CUA-AutoDebug ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">FastCUA: Developing a new fast I/O system for CUAs.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Standard computer-use runtimes
typically take roughly 2–3 seconds from issuing an action to receiving an
observation. This latency is dominated by a variety of elements, such as action execution, waiting for the
application to respond, and networking. The delay incidentally gives the application
time to process the action (e.g., open a menu), allowing the agent to observe
its effect. We therefore follow this design for our main evaluations.
However, we develop a fast I/O mode, <span id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">FastCUA</span>, by optimizing networking, action
execution, and image processing latencies (see Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Infrastructure: Technical Details ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>). FastCUA reduces action-to-observation latency to 2–28 ms, an improvement of more than an order of magnitude over typical runtimes. At this speed, a screenshot can be captured before the application has updated its UI in response to an action. We evaluate this setting to test whether lower infrastructure latency reduces overall wall time.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Implementing agents on <span id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">cua-speedrun</span>.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Since we have standardized infrastructure, new agents can be implemented with a single Python file that contains the agent loop. We also provide standard templates for various popular agents, which users can tweak directly. We provide options for both hosted evaluations and local evaluations through a single CLI call. See Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Implementing and Evaluating an Agent ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> for more details.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Results</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate 56 agent configurations on OSWorld and 21 on OSWorld2 using the
representative task sets from Sec. <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Selecting a Representative Set ‣ 2 Method ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>. These
configurations cover frontier open-weight and proprietary models, each run
through its public reference agent implementation or native computer-use API
at selected reasoning-effort settings, with the tasks and infrastructure
held fixed (Appendix <a href="#A10" title="Appendix J Experimental Details ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">J</span></a>). We validate all agent designs for correctness
through manual inspection and CUA-AutoDebug on representative tasks. For selected models, we also compare different agent
harness designs, standard and fast I/O, and single versus batched tool calls
per model response. Repeated evaluations are stable: across five seeds,
GPT-6 Astra (low) scores <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90.8\pm 1.8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90.8</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>1.8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90.8\pm 1.8</annotation></semantics></math>% on OSWorld with a mean task time
of <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="89.5\pm 2.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>89.5</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>2.2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">89.5\pm 2.2</annotation></semantics></math> s (Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Run-to-Run Variation ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Metrics.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each configuration, we report the mean verifier score, which retains
partial credit, together with the mean task time
(Sec. <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 Standardized Computer-Use Evaluation ‣ 2 Method ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>) and mean model cost per task. We report
the performance–time and performance–cost Pareto frontiers, as well as the
joint frontier over all three. Interaction turns, generated tokens, and exact completion
are defined in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Interaction and Token Measurements ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.40284v1/results_overview_multicolor_kimi_review_20260925.svg" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/330;" width="548" height="330"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span><span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Different agents define the speed and cost frontiers.</span>
Mean score vs. mean task time and model cost on OSWorld (top, 54
configs) and OSWorld2 (bottom, 19 configs), excluding MiniMax M3. Dashed lines
connect the observed Pareto-frontier points, which are circled. Colors and marker shapes
identify models, and darker shades indicate increased reasoning effort.
The plots compare complete agent configs. Costs use recorded charges or
token usage at the applicable API prices. Astra (low) uses five-seed means for each I/O setting.
Full configs and plots in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Full Evaluation Results ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Analysis</h3>

<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">No single model family dominates the frontier.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Fig. <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Metrics. ‣ 3.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Results ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows the performance–time and
performance–cost Pareto frontiers on both benchmarks. On OSWorld, the
high-performance end of the time frontier extends from Claude Opus 5 (low),
with a score of 87.6% in 86 s, through GPT-6 Astra (low), with 90.8% in
90 s, to Astra (xhigh), with 91.6% in 127 s. Gemini 3.8 Flash (low) matches the highest score and takes almost
the same time as GPT-6 Astra, but costs $0.11 rather than $0.71 per task.
At the lower-cost end, GPT-5.6 Luna (low, direct API) costs about $0.01
per task but scores 61.8%. Thus, <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">cua-speedrun</span> enables
comparison across various dimensions such as speed, cost and performance, rather than
reducing the comparison to a single model ranking.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">The Pareto frontier changes across benchmarks.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Fig. <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Metrics. ‣ 3.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Results ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> also shows that, unlike the OSWorld time frontier, the OSWorld2 time frontier
is formed entirely by GPT-6 Astra configurations. Astra (high) achieves
75.0% in 914 s, while xhigh reaches 76.9% in 1,237 s, achieving an
additional 1.9 percentage points with 35% more time. However, the cost frontier includes
other models such as Gemini 3.8 Flash (medium), which achieves 59.9% at
$2.91 per task, compared to Astra (high) at $7.39. Muse Spark 1.3
(minimal) extends the frontier to lower cost, with a score of 34.0%
at an estimated $0.39. Surprisingly, there is no open model on either the cost or the time frontier for either OSWorld or OSWorld2. Tracking these frontiers allows us to highlight the trade-off
explicitly. The preferred agent depends on both the benchmark and the
performance required within a time or cost budget, and there is no universal model family that dominates across different benchmarks.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.40284v1/results_reasoning_interactions_green_20260921.svg" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/145;" width="548" height="145"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span><span id="S3.F3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Less reasoning can make an agent slower.</span>
Gemini 3 Flash Preview at low, medium, and high effort on OSWorld. The panels show mean task time,
generated tokens including reasoning, and model calls across all 50 tasks.
Scores are 33.6%, 57.6%, and 59.6%, respectively. Medium and high effort
generate more tokens than low effort but require fewer calls and
complete tasks faster.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S3.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.40284v1/results_reasoning_green_20260921.svg" id="S3.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/193;" width="548" height="193"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span><span id="S3.F4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The useful reasoning setting changes across benchmarks.</span>
Gemini 3.8 Flash at low, medium, and high effort; labels also report mean
cost per task. Each curve keeps the model, agent harness, and execution
settings fixed. Additional reasoning brings no gain on OSWorld, whereas
moving from low to medium substantially improves OSWorld2 performance.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S3.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2609.40284v1/results_fast_io_green_20260921.png" id="S3.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/161;" width="548" height="161" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span><span id="S3.F5.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Faster I/O can be offset by more waiting and agent interaction.</span>
GPT-6 Astra (low), with normal and fast I/O. Panel (a) separates agent
time, agent-requested waits, and remaining environment processing,
averaged over five seeds per setting; error bars show the standard
deviation of mean task time across seeds. Panel (b) shows two consecutive
screenshots after opening Save As: the dialog is absent in the first
and visible in the second, requested 5.8 s later with no intervening action.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Less reasoning can sometimes make agents slower.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Fig. <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ The Pareto frontier changes across benchmarks. ‣ 3.2 Analysis ‣ 3 Results ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> compares Gemini 3 Flash Preview
at different reasoning settings on OSWorld, keeping the model and harness
fixed. Moving from low to medium effort improves the score from 33.6% to
57.6% while reducing mean task time from 492 s to 268 s. We diagnose
this as follows: at lower reasoning effort, while the model generates fewer tokens (1,598 vs.  4,125 at medium effort), it takes substantially more steps (56.0 vs. 32.5),
since most of its steps are suboptimal. For instance, the trajectories show repeated unsuccessful actions
at low effort, such as repeatedly trying to enter spreadsheet text through
key combinations instead of text entry. Counterintuitively, higher reasoning effort can therefore
shorten the interaction enough to reduce total task time, even when it
increases the number of generated tokens per step.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">More reasoning can increase time and cost without improving performance.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Fig. <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ The Pareto frontier changes across benchmarks. ‣ 3.2 Analysis ‣ 3 Results ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> compares reasoning settings within
Gemini 3.8 Flash on each benchmark. On OSWorld, low and medium reasoning both score
91.6%, but medium increases mean task time from 127 s to 250 s and
approximately doubles cost. However, the trend changes on OSWorld2: moving from low to medium
improves performance from 35.3% to 59.9%. But increasing effort further
to high adds only 0.2 percentage points while increasing time by 49%
and cost by 72%. GPT-6 Astra shows a similar dependence on the benchmark: on OSWorld, medium effort is within
2 points of xhigh at 29% less time and 15% less cost, whereas on OSWorld2,
high effort gains 7.8 points over medium for 10% more time.
The useful reasoning setting therefore depends on the
tasks as well as the model: additional reasoning can be valuable on one
(harder) benchmark and unnecessary on another (simpler) benchmark.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Faster infra can make the agent slower.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Fig. <a href="#S3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ The Pareto frontier changes across benchmarks. ‣ 3.2 Analysis ‣ 3 Results ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> compares GPT-6 Astra (low) with the normal input-output mode and
our faster input-output mode, FastCUA (Sec. <a href="#S2.SS3" title="2.3 Infrastructure ‣ 2 Method ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a> and Appendix <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Fast I/O Implementation ‣ Appendix B Infrastructure: Technical Details ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a>) across five seeds per setting. Interestingly, while the
mean environment processing time falls from 12.68 s to 0.34 s per task,
total task time increases from 89.5 s to 99.0 s. We also find
that the number of steps per trajectory increases in FastCUA. This is because fast I/O can return screenshots before an application
has updated its interface. For example, after opening Save As, the agent
receives a screenshot without the dialog and requests another screenshot
5.8 s later, which shows it open. Although theoretically a model could account for such faster I/O by using appropriate wait times
(e.g., 100   ms in this case) for
the application to update, we find that current models are not able to optimally utilize this, resulting in much higher times.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">The agent harness plays an important role in the speed–performance trade-off.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Fig. <a href="#A11.F17" title="Figure 17 ‣ Kimi benefits from batched tools at some reasoning settings. ‣ K.1 Controlled Batching Comparisons ‣ Appendix K Additional Agent Analyses ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a> compares GPT-5.6 Luna through the direct-API agent and the Codex harness on
OSWorld.
At low effort, Codex improves the score from 61.8% to 75.6%, but increases mean task time from 74 s to 145 s. The same model and reasoning setting therefore produce different performance and efficiency when used through different harnesses. At medium and high effort, the direct-API agent is instead both more accurate and faster (75.6% in 119 s vs. 67.6% in 189 s at medium; 81.6% in 161 s vs. 79.6% in 325 s at high), so neither harness is uniformly better.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px7" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Batching actions reduces task time.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each step costs a screenshot, a model call, and environment latency, so
agents that issue several actions per response (which we execute
sequentially) finish sooner: GPT-6 Astra (low) completes OSWorld tasks in
5.9 action batches on average (Table <a href="#A6.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ F.1 Five-Seed Evaluation Setup ‣ Appendix F Run-to-Run Variation ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>). Restricting
GPT-6 Astra (xhigh) to one action per response keeps its score at 91.6%
but raises mean task time from 127 s to 183 s. The benefit depends on
how well a model plans multi-action sequences, and batching alone does not
make an agent fast (Appendix <a href="#A11.SS1" title="K.1 Controlled Batching Comparisons ‣ Appendix K Additional Agent Analyses ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">K.1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px8" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Fast agents generate fewer tokens, not tokens faster.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px8.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Claude Opus 5 (low) generates 1,795 tokens per task compared with 1,579 for
GPT-6 Astra (low), while scoring 87.6% vs. 90.8%. At a common token rate
(Fig. <a href="#A5.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ E.1 Model, Harness, and Reasoning-Effort Configurations ‣ Appendix E Full Evaluation Results ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>), it falls behind the Astra configurations,
which remain the fastest high-scoring agents. Similarly, Claude Sonnet 5
(high) takes 141 s for the score that Astra (medium) reaches in 90 s,
generating <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px8.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3.5\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.5\times</annotation></semantics></math> more tokens, and Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) generates
<math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px8.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="5.6\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5.6</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.6\times</annotation></semantics></math> more tokens than at low effort and finishes <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px8.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2.7\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.7</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.7\times</annotation></semantics></math> later.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px9" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Extending to other benchmarks.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px9.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We additionally evaluate GPT-6 Astra with Codex at four reasoning settings on
MyPCBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2026a</a>)</cite> and
CUA-World <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Aggarwal et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, which test
personalized and long-horizon computer use and grade trajectories with
vision-language models rather than programmatic checks. Astra exceeds 90%
rubric scores on both (Appendix <a href="#A5.SS5" title="E.5 Reasoning Effort on MyPCBench ‣ Appendix E Full Evaluation Results ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.5</span></a>), highlighting
the need for more challenging task sets.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Practical Suggestions for Building CUAs</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Based on the analysis above, we make the following suggestions for building
efficient CUAs:</p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Choose a frontier configuration for the required performance
and budget.</span> No single configuration is best on every metric, and the
frontier shifts across benchmarks (Figs. <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Metrics. ‣ 3.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Results ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>
and <a href="#S3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 3.3 Practical Suggestions for Building CUAs ‣ 3 Results ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>), so candidates should be measured on
tasks that resemble the target workload.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Tune reasoning effort rather than setting it to an extreme.</span>
Too little reasoning can lengthen trajectories, while too much can add time
and cost without improving performance
(Figs. <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ The Pareto frontier changes across benchmarks. ‣ 3.2 Analysis ‣ 3 Results ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>
and <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ The Pareto frontier changes across benchmarks. ‣ 3.2 Analysis ‣ 3 Results ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). Start with low or medium effort and raise
it only for a measured gain.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Batch actions when intermediate screenshots are unnecessary.</span>
Fewer steps mean fewer screenshots, model calls, and environment round
trips.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reduce generated tokens and steps rather than maximizing
token rate or I/O speed.</span> Faster generation or I/O helps only if the agent
does not spend it on longer outputs or additional steps
(Fig. <a href="#S3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ The Pareto frontier changes across benchmarks. ‣ 3.2 Analysis ‣ 3 Results ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Optimize the harness alongside the model.</span> The same model and
reasoning setting can land at different points on the frontier depending
on its harness (Fig. <a href="#A11.F17" title="Figure 17 ‣ Kimi benefits from batched tools at some reasoning settings. ‣ K.1 Controlled Batching Comparisons ‣ Appendix K Additional Agent Analyses ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.40284v1/results_joint_frontier_osworld_multicolor_review_20260925.svg" id="S3.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/270;" width="548" height="270"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span><span id="S3.F6.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Choosing an agent by performance, time, and cost.</span>
Joint Pareto frontier on OSWorld; the OSWorld2 frontier is in
Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Full Evaluation Results ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>, Fig. <a href="#A5.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ E.3 OSWorld2: Performance–Time and Performance–Cost Frontiers ‣ Appendix E Full Evaluation Results ‣ cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>. Circled points are the
configurations on the Pareto frontier. Time and cost
axes are logarithmic. </figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Computer-use agent benchmarks.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The first computer-use agent benchmarks used synthetic interfaces <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. Follow-up evaluations moved to self-hosted realistic website analogs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Drouin et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, static datasets of real live website tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and live-Internet evaluations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xue et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Live, dynamic desktop benchmarks such as OSWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite> evaluate agents on real Linux desktops using programmatic verifiers, with WindowsAgentArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bonatti et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, macOSWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, iOSWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2026c</a>)</cite>, and AndroidWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rawles et al., 2025</a>)</cite> extending coverage to other platforms and professional workflows.
Recent benchmarks stress long horizons and scale, such as OSWorld 2.0 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, CUA-World from Gym-Anything <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Aggarwal et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, and Odysseys <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2026b</a>)</cite>. Another emphasis has become personal assistant evaluations, including OpenClaw-style works such as ClawBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2026b</a>)</cite>, WildClawBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ding et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, and MyPCBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2026a</a>)</cite>, which evaluate personalized computer use and digital assistants. OSWorld-Human <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abhyankar et al., 2025</a>)</cite> measures agent latency on OSWorld and compares step counts against human reference trajectories, finding that agents take longer than humans.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Computer-use agent models.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Frontier model releases have increasingly prioritized computer use <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google, 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026</a>)</cite>, with several reporting above-human scores on OSWorld-Verified. Models such as Kimi K3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kimi Team, 2026</a>)</cite>, GLM-5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">GLM-5 Team, 2026</a>)</cite>, and Muse Spark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Menghini et al., 2026</a>)</cite> have also included agentic workflows in their tech releases. Alongside these large general models, a line of work trains specialized computer-use models, including UI-TARS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, MolmoWeb <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gupta et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, Fara-1.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Awadallah et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, ScaleCUA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lv et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, and Qwen-CUA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, often in verifiable environments generated at scale <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Aggarwal et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Reproducible and efficient evaluation.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Agent evaluations are noisy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kapoor et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kapoor et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xue et al. (2025)</a></cite> showed that reported web-agent success is inflated by evaluation issues, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sahu and Pandey (2026)</a></cite> show that single-run claims are unreliable because outcomes vary substantially across data draws and run non-determinism. A separate line of work reduces the evaluation cost by selecting a small subset of a benchmark that predicts full-benchmark scores, via item response theory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Polo et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kipnis et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, sparse optimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2026a</a>)</cite>, or human validation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chowdhury et al., 2024</a>, SWE-bench Verified;)</cite>. PACE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2026</a>)</cite> predicts agentic benchmark scores from cheap, non-agentic evaluations.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we introduced <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">cua-speedrun</span>, a framework for evaluating
the performance, speed, and cost of computer-use agents under standardized
infrastructure. Our evaluations on OSWorld and OSWorld2 identify the
performance–time and performance–cost Pareto frontiers and show how these
change across benchmarks. We further find that more reasoning can reduce
task time by avoiding repeated unsuccessful actions, while faster I/O can
increase it through additional interaction. These results highlight the
need to study reasoning and interaction together when developing faster
agents. We hope <span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">cua-speedrun</span> enables the community to improve both
capability and efficiency, making computer-use agents more practical
to deploy.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSSx1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
